sections.title: 11. Interview Questions
sections.body:
### A. Conceptual Q&A

**Q1. Why is credit assignment fundamentally harder in multi-agent systems than in single-agent systems?**
A single agent has one trajectory; the error must have occurred somewhere on it. A multi-agent system has *N* trajectories plus a coordination layer, and the final answer is a function of all of them. The error could originate in any agent, propagate through several, or emerge from the interaction itself. You need explicit tracing techniques (forward, backward, counterfactual) to localize blame.

**Q2. When does a multi-agent system beat a single agent?**
When the task decomposes into genuinely different sub-skills (e.g., coding + testing + writing docs), when parallelism reduces wall-clock time, or when debate surfaces errors a single agent would commit. Multi-agent loses when the task is monolithic, when communication overhead dominates, or when agents are interchangeable (you are paying for N agents and getting 1 worth of behavior).

**Q3. What is emergent behavior in multi-agent systems, and why does it matter for eval?**
Emergent behavior is team-level behavior no individual agent exhibits: spontaneous specialization, echo chambers, sycophancy, infinite agreement loops. It matters because it is invisible to per-agent metrics — a system where every agent scores 0.95 in isolation can still produce an echo chamber. You need trajectory-level and interaction-level metrics (coordination efficiency, loop detection) to catch it.

**Q4. How do you measure coordination efficiency, and what is a bad score?**
Coordination efficiency is the fraction of inter-agent messages that advance the task. A message is redundant if it restates prior content or is a pure acknowledgment. Below 0.5 means more than half the messages are wasted chatter; below 0.3 is a structural problem, not noise.

**Q5. What is the difference between forward tracing and backward tracing for credit assignment?**
Forward tracing starts at the task and walks through the agent graph, tagging each artifact correct/incorrect; the first incorrect artifact is the origin. Backward tracing starts at the wrong final answer and walks back, asking which agent's output was the proximate cause. Forward is one-pass and identifies origin; backward is more precise about the proximate cause but may miss upstream origins.

**Q6. How would you detect a sycophancy failure in a debate system?**
Three signatures: (1) sentiment trajectory is monotonically increasing and converges to "fully agree" before the task is solved; (2) per-round token novelty is flat (no new information); (3) the critic agent's messages contain zero explicit objections. Any one is a flag; all three together is a confident diagnosis.

**Q7. Why is task success rate alone insufficient for multi-agent eval?**
Two systems can have TSR=0.9 with wildly different cost profiles, coordination quality, and robustness. One might use 2 agents and 1k tokens; the other 8 agents and 20k tokens. TSR tells you the system *works*; the other metrics tell you whether it *works well* and whether it will *keep working* under harder tasks.

**Q8. What is the specialization score, and why does low specialization matter even when TSR is high?**
Specialization score measures how behaviorally distinct agents are (low pairwise overlap in tool usage, vocabulary, or actions). Low specialization with high TSR means you are paying for N agents but getting one agent's worth of behavior — a single-agent system would match TSR at a fraction of the cost. It is an efficiency red flag, not an accuracy one.

**Q9. How do you evaluate whether a debate system converged "well" versus "prematurely"?**
Convergence is well-judged by three signals: (1) convergence rounds is well below the cap; (2) the final answer is correct; (3) at least one substantive dispute was raised and resolved during the debate. Premature convergence hits (1) but not (2) or (3) — agents agreed too fast without genuine engagement.

**Q10. What is the role of leave-one-out ablation in multi-agent eval?**
You replace each agent in turn with a trivial baseline and measure TSR change. If TSR drops sharply, that agent was carrying weight. If TSR is unchanged or improves, the agent was neutral or actively harmful. It is the most unambiguous way to measure individual agent contribution, but it is expensive (N reruns per task).

### B. Scenario-Based Questions

**Scenario**: A 3-agent system achieves 95% task success rate but has 8× the latency and 6× the token cost of a single-agent baseline that achieves 89% task success.

**Task**: Decide whether to ship the multi-agent system. Defend your answer with the metrics you would check.

**Sample Answer**: First normalize by cost: compute correct-answers-per-dollar for both systems. If the multi-agent cost-per-correct-answer is more than 2× the single-agent's, the 6-point TSR gain is rarely worth it in production. Second, check communication overhead — if above 0.5, most of the 6× cost is agents talking to each other, which is fixable. Third, check whether the TSR gain is concentrated on hard multi-step tasks: if so, ship a router that uses single-agent by default and escalates to multi-agent only when needed. Default: do not ship multi-agent as the default path; ship it as an escalation path.

**Scenario**: Two agents in your debate system keep agreeing with each other and produce wrong answers. The individual agents score 0.9 on role adherence.

**Task**: Diagnose what is happening and propose a fix.

**Sample Answer**: This is a sycophancy / echo-chamber failure. Role adherence is misleading because both agents are technically "in role" while agreeing — the critic utters critic-shaped sentences that happen to agree. Diagnose with three signals: (1) flat per-round token novelty confirms no new information; (2) near-zero explicit objections per round confirms sycophancy; (3) check the system prompts — if the critic is told to "collaborate" or "be constructive", that is the cause. Fixes: rewrite the critic's prompt to require at least one objection per round; assign it the adversarial role of steelmanning the opposite position; or cap consecutive agreements and auto-terminate if exceeded.

**Scenario**: Your multi-agent coding system (planner, coder, tester, reviewer) passes all short tasks (under 100 lines) but fails on long tasks (over 500 lines).

**Task**: Debug the failure using multi-agent eval techniques.

**Sample Answer**: This is almost certainly an information-loss or cascading-error problem that scales with task length. Run forward tracing on 10 failed long-task trajectories: tag each agent's output correct/incorrect against per-step ground truth. The likely pattern is that the planner's output is correct but information degrades at each handoff — by the time the tester sees the plan, key constraints are lost. Confirm with the information-loss metric per handoff pair. If loss scales with plan length, the fix is structural: have the planner emit a structured spec (not prose) that downstream agents reference by key. Also check cascading error rate: if small upstream errors propagate to final failure on long tasks, the tester is not catching them — add intermediate checkpoints where the tester validates partial work mid-task.

**Scenario**: You are evaluating a CrewAI crew with 4 agents. The crew-level TSR is 0.78, but per-task output quality averages 0.91. The final answer is wrong even though every individual task output looks good.

**Task**: Identify the most likely failure mode and the metric that would confirm it.

**Sample Answer**: The gap between high per-task quality (0.91) and lower final TSR (0.78) is the signature of an *integration* failure, not a per-agent failure. The likely cause is information loss or mis-synthesis at the final handoff — the last agent receives good inputs but combines them incorrectly. Confirm by computing information loss at the final handoff (do all key facts from prior task outputs appear in the final answer?) and by running a counterfactual: manually construct the ideal final answer from the task outputs and compare. If the counterfactual is correct and the actual is wrong, the final agent is the culprit. Also check its role effectiveness — it may be overloaded with both synthesis and writing.

**Scenario**: A LangGraph multi-agent system hits the maximum-rounds cap on 30% of tasks. Stakeholders want to raise the cap.

**Task**: Recommend whether to raise the cap, and what to measure first.

**Sample Answer**: Do not raise the cap yet. Hitting the round cap 30% of the time is a *symptom* — the system is not converging, and raising the cap will increase cost without fixing convergence. First, log which cycles are traversed repeatedly: LangGraph's state graph lets you diff state per node visit, so identify the node pair (A→B→A) that loops. Second, check the cycle's exit condition — if it depends on a state field that never updates, that is a logic bug, not a depth bug. Third, check convergence rounds on the 70% of tasks that terminate naturally: if they finish in 2–3 rounds, the cap is fine and the 30% are genuine non-convergence cases needing a fix (better exit condition, forced termination on no-state-change, or a different topology). Only then consider raising the cap, and only for genuinely hard tasks.
